passages.happening:
Jesus comes back from the Jordan “full of the Holy Spirit” (verse 1), and the Spirit leads him into the wilderness. For forty days the devil tests him. He eats nothing, and at the end he is hungry.

The devil says, “If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (verse 3). Jesus answers from Scripture: “Man shall not live on bread alone” (verse 4).

The devil shows him all the kingdoms of the world in an instant. He says they have been handed over to him, and he can give them to anyone. “So if You worship me, it will all be Yours” (verse 7). Jesus answers, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (verse 8).

Last, the devil takes him to Jerusalem, sets him on the highest point of the temple, and quotes a psalm: God will send angels to catch him. Jesus answers, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (verse 12). The devil leaves him “until an opportune time” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells this story too, and the notes on Matthew 4 explain it more fully: the word that means both ‘tempted’ and ‘tested’, the forty years of Israel in the desert, and the pinnacle of the temple. Here it is enough to see what Luke does differently.

First, the order. Matthew ends on a mountain with the kingdoms of the world. Luke ends in Jerusalem, at the temple. That fits Luke's whole book. It begins in the temple, with Zechariah at the altar. From 9:51 Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, and the book ends with the disciples in the temple courts. Scholars are not sure which Gospel kept the order of the first telling. Each order makes its own point.

Second, the place in the story. Luke puts his family tree of Jesus just before this scene, and it ends with ‘the son of Adam, the son of God’ (3:38). Then the devil says, ‘If You are the Son of God’. Adam, God's son, was tested in a garden full of food and fell. Jesus is tested in a desert, hungry, and holds firm.

Third, the boast. Only Luke has the devil say of the kingdoms, “it has been relinquished to me” (verse 6). Luke reports the claim. He does not say it is true. Jesus does not argue about it. He simply refuses to bow.

Fourth, the ending. In Luke the devil leaves only ‘until an opportune time’. He comes back. When the plot to kill Jesus begins, Luke says, “Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve” (22:3).
passages.ot:
All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy, where Moses reminds Israel of its forty years in the wilderness. “The LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you” (Deuteronomy 8:2). The answers are Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:13 and 6:16. Israel grumbled for bread, turned to other gods, and tested God at Massah. Jesus, at each point, answers as Israel should have.

The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12. But he leaves out a few words. The psalm says the angels will guard you “in all your ways” (Psalm 91:11), the ways of a person walking with God. The devil drops that phrase and turns a promise of care into a dare.
passages.hard:
Was the temptation real, if Jesus was the Son of God? Christians have answered in two ways. Many have taught that he could not sin, because of who he is, and yet that he truly felt the pull of temptation, more fully than those who give in early. Others have taught that, as a man, he was able not to sin, which is different from being unable to sin. Both confess with Hebrews that he was tempted “in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). The creeds do not settle the finer question.

A word of care about fasting. Jesus' forty days were a unique moment. Christians have fasted in many ways, but no one should go without food in a way that harms the body. Ask a doctor first, and if not eating has become a struggle for you, please talk to someone you trust and a health professional.
passages.asks: Every test asked Jesus to prove he was God's Son on the devil's terms: by meeting his own needs, by grabbing power without the cross, by forcing God to show himself. Where are you tempted to take a short cut to something good? Being tempted is not a sin. Jesus was tempted too, and he knows how it feels.

passages.happening:
Jesus returns to Galilee “in the power of the Spirit” (verse 14). He teaches in the synagogues, and everyone praises him.

Then he comes to Nazareth, the village where he grew up. On the Sabbath he goes to the synagogue, as he always did. He stands up to read, and he is handed the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it and finds the place where it says:

“The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor” (verses 18-19).

He rolls up the scroll, gives it back to the attendant, and sits down. Every eye is on him. Then he says, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew also tell of Jesus being turned away at Nazareth (Mark 6:1-6; Matthew 13:53-58), but later in the story and without the reading. Only Luke tells it this way. He puts it at the very start of Jesus' public work, like a title page for everything that follows. Luke knew it was not the first event in time: in verse 23 Jesus mentions what he has already done in Capernaum. Luke puts it first because it explains the rest.

What was a synagogue service like? We know less than we would like. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem, set up by a priest named Theodotus, says his synagogue was built for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments. Most scholars date it before the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, though its date is debated. Acts tells of a Sabbath service with “the reading from the Law and the Prophets”, after which the leaders invited visitors to speak (Acts 13:15). So a reading from the five books of Moses, then one from the Prophets, then teaching, is a fair picture. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, later than the Gospels, says that a reader of the Prophets could skip from place to place, but a reader of the Law could not (Megillah 4:4). Whether set readings were fixed in Jesus' day is not known. Luke's words ‘He found the place’ may mean that Jesus chose this passage himself.

The reader stood out of respect for Scripture. The teacher sat down to teach. So when Jesus sits, everyone knows he is about to speak. A scroll was a long roll of leather or papyrus; finding a place near the end of Isaiah meant winding through most of it.

‘Anointed’ is the key word. Kings and priests in Israel were marked out for God's work by having oil poured on them. The Hebrew word for ‘anointed one’ gives us ‘Messiah’, and the Greek word gives us ‘Christ’. Jesus has been anointed not with oil but with the Spirit, who came on him at his baptism (3:22). Peter later says that God “anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38).
passages.ot:
The reading joins two passages of Isaiah. Most of it is Isaiah 61:1-2. The line ‘to release the oppressed’ comes from Isaiah 58:6, where God says the fast he wants is “to set the oppressed free” (Isaiah 58:6). Luke follows the old Greek translation of Isaiah, which is why it has ‘recovery of sight to the blind’, where the Hebrew, in our Isaiah, reads “freedom to the prisoners” (Isaiah 61:1). Isaiah's words ‘to bind up the brokenhearted’ are missing from the oldest copies of Luke. Later copies have them, and so does the King James Version.

In Isaiah, the speaker is a messenger sent to God's people after the exile, when the land lay in ruins. He brings good news to the broken and the poor.

Notice where Jesus stops. Isaiah's sentence goes on: “and the day of our God's vengeance” (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus stops in the middle of the line, rolls up the scroll, and sits down. Many readers have seen meaning in this. The time he announces is a time of favour first.

‘The year of the Lord's favor’ and ‘liberty’ call up the Jubilee. In Leviticus 25, every fiftieth year was to be a year of release: “proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants” (Leviticus 25:10). Israelites who had sold themselves into service went free, and family land went back to its family. The land was God's, not theirs to sell for ever (Leviticus 25:23). There is no clear record that Israel ever kept the Jubilee in full, and scholars debate whether it was kept at all. But the hope behind it grew. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, written before Jesus' day, a text called 11Q13 joins Leviticus 25 and Isaiah 61 to describe a great release at the end of days.
passages.hard:
What does ‘good news to the poor’ mean? Christians have heard it in two ways, and both carry real weight.

Some stress the spiritual meaning. The Greek word for ‘liberty’ and ‘release’ in verse 18 is the same word Luke uses elsewhere for ‘forgiveness’, as in “forgiveness of sins” (24:47). On this reading the captives are people bound by sin and the devil, and the blind are those who cannot see God. Luke's Gospel is full of that release: sins forgiven, demons driven out, eyes opened to who Jesus is.

Others stress the social meaning. Luke means the poor, not only the ‘poor in spirit’. His Gospel is full of real poor people, real widows, real beggars and real blind men. A Jubilee was about debts, slaves and land. On this reading, the good news reaches the body and the purse, and a church that ignores the poor has not heard it.

Luke will not let either reading swallow the other. The same Jesus forgives a paralysed man and then makes him walk (5:20-25). When John later asks if Jesus is the one, Jesus answers with a list that runs from “The blind receive sight” to “the good news is preached to the poor” (7:22). Nor does Luke turn the reading into the programme of a political party, of the left or the right. It is the announcement that God has come, in Jesus, to set people free.
passages.asks: Jesus said ‘today’. Not someday, not when life gets better. Where do you need to hear that God's favour has reached you now? And who around you is poor, held captive, or unable to see, who needs the good news to reach them in both word and deed?

passages.t: No prophet is welcome at home
passages.happening:
At first everyone speaks well of Jesus. They are amazed at his gracious words. Then they ask, “Isn't this the son of Joseph?” (verse 22).

Jesus knows what they are thinking. They will quote the proverb, “Physician, heal yourself!” (verse 23), and demand that he do in his home town what he did in Capernaum. He says, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown” (verse 24).

Then he reminds them of two stories from their own Scriptures. In Elijah's day there were many widows in Israel during a long famine, yet Elijah was sent to none of them, “but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon” (verse 26). In Elisha's day there were many lepers in Israel, yet the only one cleansed was Naaman the Syrian.

The synagogue erupts in rage. They drive him out of the town to the edge of the hill it is built on, to throw him over the cliff. “But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
‘Isn't this the son of Joseph?’ may begin as admiration and turn into a doubt: we know this man, we know his family, who does he think he is? Familiarity can make it hard to hear.

‘Physician, heal yourself’ was a proverb. Here it means: look after your own first. If he has done wonders elsewhere, his own town has a right to them.

A play on words links verses 19 and 24. The ‘year of the Lord's favor’ uses the Greek word for welcome or acceptable. The prophet who announces it is not ‘accepted’, the same word, in his home town.

The two examples would have stung. Zarephath was in Sidon, Phoenician country, the homeland of Queen Jezebel, who led Israel into the worship of Baal (1 Kings 16:31). Naaman was the commander of the army of Aram, Israel's enemy (2 Kings 5:1). God's prophets had passed over Israelites in need and helped foreigners. Jesus is saying that God's mercy has never been the property of one town or one people.

Luke does not tell us how Jesus walked away. He simply did. His time had not yet come. Later he will be led out of another city, Jerusalem, to die.
passages.ot:
In 1 Kings 17, God sends Elijah to a widow in Zarephath during a drought. She shares her last flour and oil, and they do not run out. Later Elijah raises her son. She says, “Now I know that you are a man of God” (1 Kings 17:24).

In 2 Kings 5, Naaman comes to Elisha, dips seven times in the Jordan, and is made clean. He says, “there is no God in all the earth except in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15).

Jesus speaks of three and a half years of famine. 1 Kings 18:1 speaks of “the third year of the drought”, counting from an earlier point; James 5:17 also gives “three and a half years”. Prophets rejected by their own people are an old theme in Israel's Scriptures. Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:15), and later lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 38:6).
passages.hard:
Why were they so angry? It was not one thing. They wanted signs and did not get them. A local boy was making great claims. And worst of all, he reminded them that in their own Scriptures God had sent his prophets to outsiders while insiders went without. That hurts anyone who thinks God owes them.

This passage has sometimes been preached as if the people of Nazareth stood for all Jews, against a kind Jesus who loved the Gentiles. That is wrong. Jesus is a Jew in a synagogue on the Sabbath, reading Israel's own Scriptures. The stories of the widow and Naaman come from Israel's prophets, who told them against their own people's pride. The crowd's rage is the rage of one town on one day, not a verdict on the Jewish people. Luke's book page says more. The warning is for every insider, including the church: those who feel most at home with Jesus may be the slowest to let his mercy go to others.
passages.asks: The people of Nazareth thought they knew Jesus too well to listen to him. Is there a familiar part of your faith you have stopped hearing? And who do you secretly think God should help less than you?

passages.t: A word with authority in Capernaum
passages.happening:
Jesus goes down to Capernaum, a town by the lake in Galilee, and teaches on the Sabbath. The people are astonished, “because His message had authority” (verse 32).

In the synagogue is a man with an unclean spirit. It cries out, “What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us?” (verse 34). It says it knows who he is: the Holy One of God.

Jesus rebukes it: “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” (verse 35). The demon throws the man down in front of them all and comes out “without harming him” (verse 35). Everyone is amazed. What is this word, they ask, that commands unclean spirits with authority and power? News of him spreads everywhere.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene almost the same way (Mark 1:21-28), and the notes on Mark 1 tell about Capernaum's synagogue and what an ‘unclean spirit’ meant. Capernaum, unlike Nazareth, welcomes him.

Luke adds one tender detail: the demon came out ‘without harming him’. Luke cares about the man, not only about the power.

Jesus uses no ritual and no charm. He uses a word, and only a word. That is what amazes the crowd.

Notice too that the spirit knows who Jesus is, and Jesus silences it. He does not want his name announced by a demon.
passages.ot: ‘The Holy One’ is how the Old Testament often speaks of God. Isaiah calls him “the Holy One of Israel” again and again (Isaiah 1:4). Aaron is called “the holy one of the LORD” (Psalm 106:16). A spirit that is unclean meets the one who is holy, and it cannot stay.
passages.hard: Was this a real evil spirit, or an illness people did not understand? Ancient people did know the difference between sickness and possession. Luke himself keeps them apart: at sunset Jesus heals the sick by laying hands on them, and demons come out of many (verses 40-41). Christians today hold that evil is real and personal, while also using medicine for illness. Wisdom avoids both blaming every illness on demons and treating evil as a myth.
passages.asks: The crowd asked, ‘What is this word?’ Jesus' word still has authority. Is there something that holds you that you think is too strong for him? He does not need a ritual. He needs only to speak, and he does not do harm when he sets people free.

passages.t: A fever, and a town at the door
passages.happening:
Jesus leaves the synagogue and goes to Simon's house. Simon's mother-in-law has a high fever, and they ask Jesus to help her. He stands over her, rebukes the fever, and it leaves her. She gets up at once and begins to serve them.

At sunset people bring everyone who is sick to Jesus. “Laying His hands on each one, He healed them” (verse 40). Demons come out of many people, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” (verse 41). But he rebukes them and will not let them speak, because they know he is the Christ.
passages.hearers:
Simon is the fisherman later called Peter. Luke mentions his house before telling of his call in chapter 5, perhaps because his readers already knew who Simon was.

Luke, whom Paul called “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), says the fever was ‘high’. And Luke says Jesus ‘rebuked’ the fever, the same word used for the demon in verse 35 and the demons in verse 41. He treats sickness as something that should not be there, which Jesus orders away.

Why wait until sunset? The Jewish day ran from sunset to sunset, so the Sabbath ended at dusk. Carrying a load counted as work on the Sabbath. Once the sun went down, people could carry their sick through the streets. The whole town came.

Only Luke says Jesus laid his hands ‘on each one’. A crowd could have been healed with one word. Jesus touched them one by one.
passages.ot: The prophet Jeremiah told the people not to carry a load on the Sabbath day (Jeremiah 17:21-22). That is why the sick had to wait until evening. The psalm says the LORD “heals all your diseases” (Psalm 103:3). The Christ the demons name is the anointed one of Psalm 2.
passages.hard:
Why did Jesus silence the demons when they told the truth about him? Luke says it was ‘because they knew He was the Christ’. Jesus would not take his title from evil spirits. People were to come to know him by what he said and did, and by the cross, not by a demon's shout. Many people also expected a Christ who would be a warrior king, and Jesus did not want that idea spread before people could see what kind of Christ he was.

Not everyone who prays is healed as these people were. The notes on the next chapter say plainly what the Bible does and does not teach about sickness and faith.
passages.asks: The woman who was healed got up and served. And Jesus, with a crowd at the door, touched each person. Do you believe Jesus sees you one by one, not as part of a crowd? And when God has helped you, whom could you serve?

passages.happening:
At daybreak Jesus goes out to a solitary place. The crowds look for him, find him, and try to keep him from leaving.

But he tells them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent” (verse 43). And he goes on preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
passages.hearers:
Capernaum wants to keep Jesus for itself. Nazareth wanted him to do miracles for them. Jesus belongs to neither town. He has been sent to many.

This is the first time in Luke that Jesus speaks of ‘the kingdom of God’: God's rule breaking into the world through him. The verb ‘to preach the good news’ is the same one he read from Isaiah in verse 18, and ‘sent’ echoes ‘He has sent Me’ in the same reading. The chapter ends where the Nazareth reading began.

Verse 44 says ‘Judea’, though Jesus is in Galilee. The oldest copies of Luke read ‘Judea’; many later copies read ‘Galilee’, as Mark does (Mark 1:39), which is why the King James Version has ‘Galilee’. Many think Luke uses ‘Judea’ here in a wide sense, for the whole land of the Jews, as he does in 1:5.
passages.ot: In Isaiah, the messenger who brings good news says, “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news” (Isaiah 52:7). Jesus is that messenger, and he must keep walking. The word ‘sent’ also recalls the prophets, whom God sent to his people again and again (Jeremiah 7:25).
passages.hard: Was it unkind of Jesus to leave a town that wanted him? It can look that way. But he was not leaving them without anything; he had healed their sick and taught them. He was refusing to become one town's possession. His prayer at dawn and his choice to move on go together. Luke shows Jesus going off to pray again and again before he decides what to do.
passages.asks: Jesus started his day alone with God, and then said no to a good thing so he could do the thing he was sent for. What are you trying to keep Jesus for, that he means for others too? And what might you need to say no to, to do what God has given you to do?
